title: The Apartment
synopsis: An office worker, a key lent to bosses, a sad elevator girl, and a New Year's Eve that finally chooses a person.

nodes.text: Ten past nine, and Kirkeby has your apartment until eleven, per the schedule you keep in a desk drawer like a man running a small hotel. It's forty degrees out. You sit on a bench in the park with your hat on your knees, catching a cold, rehearsing the sentence you will not say to him tomorrow.

choices.consequence: You give him the extra hour and get in at midnight to two glasses, one lipstick, and the window left open on purpose.
You knock on your own door and a man in your bathrobe asks for fifteen minutes. You give him twenty. You always give twenty.

nodes.text: Four department heads have written to Personnel about you in a single week, which is statistically remarkable for a man on nineteen with no discernible accomplishments. Mr. Sheldrake would like to see you. Your name is on his calendar, spelled correctly. Twenty-seven floors up, somebody has finally noticed the arrangement, and it is going to be handed to you as a compliment.

choices.consequence: You say thank you four times running. Somewhere in the fourth one you hear yourself, and you keep smiling anyway.
You pause half a second before answering. That half second is the entire extent of your rebellion this decade and nobody notices it but you.

nodes.text: Miss Kubelik runs car number two and says good morning in a way that costs you the rest of the ride. Your hat is off before the doors close. You have four remarks prepared. You deploy one — something about the weather, factually incorrect — and she laughs at it, which will carry you through to Thursday.

choices.consequence: You ask her to a show Thursday and she says yes before you've finished the sentence. You ride to nineteen without touching a single button.
You say 'nineteen, please,' as though you don't know the floor. She says it back. That's the whole conversation for another month.

nodes.text: She snaps a compact open in the elevator and the glass in the lid is cracked across one corner. You have seen that crack before. It was on your rug at two in the morning on the twelfth of November, and you handed it back to a man who already had his hat on.

choices.consequence: The floor indicator keeps counting and you keep looking straight at it. Nineteen takes an extraordinarily long time to arrive.
You study your shoes and make a remark about the humidity. She agrees about the humidity. You are both very good at this.

nodes.text: Glass walls, a desk the size of a rowboat, and a family photograph angled so that visitors can see it. He calls you buddy boy. He knows about the key. He isn't angry about the key — he'd simply like exclusive use of it, and in exchange there's a position on twenty-seven with a name plate and a window that opens.

choices.consequence: You ask for the title in writing and have it in six minutes. You have now sold the same apartment twice and gone up a floor doing it.
You say no once, quietly, and he waits. The silence does work he pays other men to do. Your hand goes to the key by itself.

nodes.text: She's late and then she isn't late, and she arrives in a coat that's too good and a hat with a feather she keeps touching. She apologizes for something she doesn't explain. Her eyes are red in a way she has powdered over twice. You don't ask. There are nine things in this booth you don't ask.

choices.consequence: You let the silence be hers and order for both of you. She notices that you did. Somehow that's worse than if she hadn't.
You do six minutes of material about the twenty-seventh floor and get two real laughs, then grade yourself on it the whole way home.

nodes.text: The office party is paper cups and a man from Accounting doing a conga past the water cooler. Miss Olsen, four martinis in, tells you a thing about Sheldrake with a smile that has a knife inside it. Later you find Miss Kubelik at a dark desk on nineteen, fixing her face in a cracked compact.

choices.consequence: You sit on the edge of the desk and say nothing for a full minute. She hands you the compact so that you can see yourself in it.
You do the bit about the executive washroom key. She laughs one syllable, and it is the loneliest sound on the nineteenth floor.

nodes.text: You come home at one with a bottle, a paper hat, and a girl from a bar you left in the taxi. The bedroom light is on. There's a coat over your chair, an empty bottle of your sleeping pills on the nightstand, and Miss Kubelik breathing at a rate slow enough to count. You count it. Twice.

choices.consequence: You go through the wall to Dreyfuss in your socks. It takes four seconds and costs you the entire story you've been telling about yourself.
You stand in the doorway eleven seconds hoping this resolves itself. Eleven seconds is the longest you have ever been a coward.

nodes.text: Dreyfuss comes through the wall in a dressing gown, slaps her awake, walks her up and down, and works on her two hours with coffee and profanity. Between rounds he looks at you — the man with the parties, the girls, the noise every other night — and tells you to be a mensch. He means it kindly. It goes in like a nail.

choices.consequence: You start explaining about the key and the floors and the arrangement, and hear exactly how it sounds out loud for the first time.
You let him think it's your fault, which is cheaper than the truth and, in every way that counts by morning, accurate.

nodes.text: Day two. She's on the couch in your bathrobe and you're straining spaghetti through a tennis racket, because you own no colander and are not about to explain that. You make meatballs. You talk about nothing for six hours: the racket, your old landlady, a horse you bet on in 1958 that is still running.

choices.consequence: You keep the room light for four straight hours. She laughs at the racket. Neither of you goes anywhere near Tuesday night.
You let the radio do the talking and hand her things before she asks. By evening she's telling you about her sister in Rockville.

nodes.text: He telephones from a booth in Jersey with a hand on his tie, which you can somehow hear. Spring, he says. He'll tell his wife in the spring. He has been saying spring for two Christmases. She listens with the receiver against her ear and her eyes on your rug, and says all right in the voice of a woman signing for a package.

choices.consequence: You decide, out of some reflex you can't name, to hope on her behalf. It's the stupidest position in the room and you hold it.
You say nothing and set the coffee down a little hard. She hears your entire opinion in the noise the cup makes.

nodes.text: Gin rummy on the coffee table, day three, and she is beating you badly. You keep the deck moving because a hand of cards is a reason for a person to stay in a chair. She discards a queen without looking at it. You pick it up. Neither of you mentions that she has nowhere to be.

choices.consequence: You throw two hands so obviously that she calls it out. She wins the next one anyway, on merit, and says so.
You play it straight and lose by ninety points, which is the first honest transaction conducted in this apartment in two years.

nodes.text: Dreyfuss will sign that it was an accident, that she was a guest, that nothing here requires a police report on Christmas. He does it for you and does not pretend it's free. Meanwhile Mrs. Lieberman on the ground floor has developed an opinion, and the fourth floor has heard the version with the ambulance in it.

choices.consequence: You tell Dreyfuss the truth about whose girl she is. He takes it in, nods once, and never raises the subject again.
You let the building keep the version where you're the villain. It's simpler, it's cheaper, and it fits you like a borrowed coat.

nodes.text: Twenty-seventh floor: corner desk, a name plate with a middle initial you have never once used, and a key to the executive washroom that is heavier than the key to your own apartment. Sheldrake hands it over personally, in front of people. You are thirty-two years old and you have arrived here by way of a spare bedroom.

choices.consequence: You take the key, shake his hand, and go and wash your hands in a private bathroom with a towel service and no mirror you like.
You say you'd rather stay on nineteen. He laughs for four seconds, decides it's a joke, and puts the key in your pocket himself.

nodes.text: He arrives at the party with Miss Olsen on his arm, which is a decision, since Miss Olsen kept his calendar for four years and knows which hotels take cash. She watches him work the room. She watches him do the joke about the reindeer that he does every single December. She is counting something.

choices.consequence: You stand by the punch bowl and watch a woman decide something. It takes her one drink and part of a second.
You ask him, in a room full of people, how his wife is keeping. He says fine, warmly, and moves you aside by the elbow.

nodes.text: Four years of it, boiled down and delivered to Mrs. Sheldrake in one telephone call, in a level voice, from a desk on twenty-seven. Miss Olsen does not raise her voice once. She has the dates. She has the names, all but one, which she keeps back, because the girl from the elevator is only twenty-four.

choices.consequence: You bring her a coffee she didn't ask for. She says she isn't sorry, twice, which is once more than a person says who isn't.
You take the long way past the filing cabinets and hear the entire call regardless. Everyone on twenty-seven hears the entire call.

nodes.text: New Year's Eve, five o'clock, and he's in your doorway with his hat in his hands asking for the apartment one more time. Tonight, just tonight, he's got a table booked and a girl who thinks she's being taken somewhere. He asks the way a man asks for a stapler. The girl is Miss Kubelik. He doesn't use her name.

choices.consequence: You say no and mean it, and find your voice steadier than expected, which surprises precisely one person in the doorway.
Your hand is in your pocket before your mouth can catch it. Two years of training, expressed in one small movement.

nodes.text: You set a key on his blotter and he picks it up and says thanks, buddy boy — then reads the tag. It's the washroom key. Twenty-seven's, brass, heavier. He explains patiently that you've made a mistake, and you tell him you're giving notice on the apartment, the job, and the arrangement, in roughly that order.

choices.consequence: You take your hat and the cover off your adding machine and go, past nineteen desks, and not one of them looks up.
You stop at the door long enough to let him get one sentence out about being reasonable. It's a bad sentence. It helps enormously.

nodes.text: Half a life fits in one suitcase and a hat box: the tennis racket, four shirts, a bowler, a bottle of the good stuff you never opened for anything. The lamp stays on because you'll need to see to lock up. It's ten to twelve and somewhere outside a hundred thousand people are counting. Then, a knock.

choices.consequence: You cross the room in four steps with a bottle in your hand and no idea which face you are about to be wearing.
You stand still and let it be Mrs. Lieberman about the noise. It is not Mrs. Lieberman. The knocking stops. Then it starts again.

nodes.text: She ran most of nineteen blocks in a coat and a good hat, having left a table, a bottle, and a man in the middle of a sentence on Fifty-Second Street. She's on the bottom step getting her breath back. She looks up at you and says, mostly to herself, that she's a little out of practice at this.

choices.consequence: You move out of the doorway and let her come up under her own steam, which is exactly the right amount of nothing to do.
You hold the door and don't deliver the speech you wrote on a park bench in November. Good. It was a terrible speech.

nodes.text: She takes off her coat, sits on the floor by the coffee table, and finds the deck in the drawer without being told which drawer. You open your mouth to say the whole thing — the promotion, the key, two years of it, all of it. She picks up the cards, looks at you, and tells you to shut up and deal.

choices.consequence: You deal. Ten cards each, one turned up, and the entire conversation gets postponed roughly a year, which suits everybody in the room.
You say it anyway, badly, in the wrong order. She lets you finish, then takes the deck and deals the hand herself.
You put the cards down, fetch two glasses, and open the bottle you were saving for an occasion which has now, technically, arrived.

nodes.text: The cards keep falling. Neither of you says the sentence for a year, and by then it has been said so many other ways that saying it would be redundant. You lose at gin approximately nine hundred times. Dreyfuss, through the wall, hears laughing at two in the morning and, for once in his life, does not come over. The building had a pool going. Mrs. Lieberman took it.

You start Monday at a firm across town, with a reference letter Sheldrake dictated through his teeth. Smaller desk, no washroom key, a boss who does not know your address and has no reason to learn it. You take a place on the fourth floor with a lock nobody else has been handed. By every measure the twenty-seventh floor would use, it's a smaller life. You sleep in it every single night.

She takes a lease on a place off Ninth with eleven tables and a coffee urn that sounds like a freight train coming in. You keep the books and bus tables at weekends, badly. The spaghetti strainer hangs over the counter where the good glasses should go, and every regular gets told the story — her version, in which you come out considerably better than you did.
